title: New Spectrum: 6 GHz and 320 MHz
summary: Wi-Fi 6E opened the 6 GHz band; Wi-Fi 7 adds channels twice as wide inside it.

opener.promise: A wide new band, free of older devices
opener.problem: Crowded older bands cap capacity, however many access points you add.

beats.heading: Too many devices, too few lanes

caption.headline: Too many devices, too few lanes
caption.takeaway: Older bands are crowded and slowed by [[legacy-device|legacy devices]]; adding access points eventually stops helping.

beats.body:
On a busy medical-surgical floor, every badge, pump, monitor and workstation shares the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands — along with older devices, guest phones and the unit next door.

Those bands only fit a handful of wide channels. Older [[legacy-device|legacy devices]] send more slowly, so they hold the channel longer for the same data, and mixed networks add compatibility overhead that every device on the channel pays for.
beats.bottomLine: Adding more access points in crowded bands eventually stops helping; capacity is limited by the spectrum itself.
beats.sceneDescription: Three roads leave an access point, one per band, each drawn as wide as its band. The narrow 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz roads are jammed: gray trucks for older devices crawl along and hold up the cars behind them, while the much wider 6 GHz road beside them sits unlit and empty.

callout.title: Why the old bands run out
points: The 2.4 and 5 GHz bands fit only a handful of wide channels
[[legacy-device|Older devices]] send slowly and hold the channel longer
Guest phones and neighboring units crowd the same channels

beats.heading: Wi-Fi 6E opens a new band

caption.headline: A new band, wider than the rest combined
caption.takeaway: Wi-Fi 6E opened 1200 MHz{{us-6ghz-total}} in the US, free of older devices{{6ghz-no-legacy}}.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 6E opened the 6 GHz band to Wi-Fi {{wifi6e-6ghz-origin}}. In the United States that adds 1200 MHz of spectrum {{us-6ghz-total}}, more than the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands combined.

Only Wi-Fi 6E and newer devices can use it {{6ghz-no-legacy}}, so no slow [[legacy-device|legacy devices]] hold up the traffic. More room means more channels, so neighboring access points compete less.
beats.bottomLine: 6 GHz is the largest block of new Wi-Fi spectrum in a generation, and only newer devices can use it.
beats.sceneDescription: The 6 GHz road lights up. Drawn to the same frequency scale, it is wider than the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz roads together, and no older devices travel on it.

questions.q: Will our existing devices use the new band?
questions.a: Only devices built for Wi-Fi 6E or later can operate in 6 GHz{{6ghz-no-legacy}}. Older devices stay on 2.4 and 5 GHz, and still benefit because capable devices move off those bands.

questions.q: Does this work outside the United States?
questions.a: Rules vary by country. The CEPT harmonized band in Europe is the lower part, 5945–6425 MHz{{eu-6ghz-band}}, so fewer wide channels fit. Check each regulator before designing.

Indoors, low-power access points may use the whole US band{{fcc-lpi}}. Standard power allows higher power on part of it, under automated frequency coordination{{fcc-sp-afc}}, and Cisco supports it on both management platforms{{cisco-afc-standard-power}}.

callout.title: What 6 GHz adds
points: 1200 MHz of new spectrum for Wi-Fi in the US{{us-6ghz-total}}
Only Wi-Fi 6E and newer devices can use it{{6ghz-no-legacy}}
More channels, so neighboring access points compete less

cisco.text: Cisco networks support standard-power 6 GHz through AFC, on Cisco wireless controllers and in the Meraki dashboard{{cisco-afc-standard-power}}.

beats.heading: Wi-Fi 7: lanes twice as wide

caption.headline: Twice the widest channel
caption.takeaway: Wi-Fi 7’s 320 MHz channels{{eht-max-width}} move big imaging files faster; plan where to use them.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 6E’s widest channel is 160 MHz {{he-max-width}}. Wi-Fi 7 doubles it to 320 MHz {{eht-max-width}} {{width-320-vs-160}}, so one transmission can carry about twice as much data, on devices that support it.

Wide channels are scarce: indoors, the US band fits only three of them {{us-6ghz-channels-320}}. They suit imaging and procedure rooms more than crowded floors. Walls also weaken 6 GHz signals more than the older bands {{6ghz-building-loss}}, so a site survey decides where access points go.
beats.bottomLine: Use 320 MHz channels{{eht-max-width}} where big files move, plan narrower ones on dense floors, and survey before placing access points.
beats.sceneDescription: The 6 GHz road is split in two. On the left, the earlier generation’s seven 160 MHz lanes {{us-6ghz-channels-160}} carry mid-sized vehicles; on the right, Wi-Fi 7’s three 320 MHz lanes {{us-6ghz-channels-320}} carry trucks twice as wide. Choosing Wi-Fi 6 closes the left half, because Wi-Fi 6 devices cannot use 6 GHz.

callout.title: Why Wi-Fi 7 is faster here
points: Its widest channel is twice Wi-Fi 6E’s{{width-320-vs-160}}
Big imaging files finish sooner, freeing [[airtime|airtime]]
Only three such channels fit indoors in the US{{us-6ghz-channels-320}}

questions.q: Why not use the widest channels everywhere?
questions.a: Only three fit in the US band{{us-6ghz-channels-320}}, so neighboring access points would overlap. Dense floors usually run narrower channels and keep the widest for lightly shared areas such as imaging rooms.

questions.q: Do we need more access points for the new band?
questions.a: Possibly in some areas. Walls weaken 6 GHz signals more than lower bands{{6ghz-building-loss}}, so a site survey decides placement. Run the survey before you budget.

cisco.text: Cisco controllers assign channels up to 160 MHz by default; 320 MHz has to be turned on for 6 GHz{{cisco-320-opt-in}}. Under US standard power, Cisco’s guidance notes only one 320 MHz channel fits{{cisco-320-us-sp-one}}.

beats.heading: More than twice the channels

caption.headline: More than twice the channels
caption.takeaway: In the US, 6 GHz holds 59 channels of 20 MHz{{us-6ghz-channels-20}}; 5 GHz holds 25{{us-5ghz-channels-20}}.

callout.title: Why more channels matter
points: Neighboring access points can each get a channel of their own
Fewer access points share a channel, so each waits less for [[airtime|airtime]]
Only Wi-Fi 6E and newer devices use 6 GHz{{6ghz-no-legacy}}

beats.body:
Counted in channels of 20 MHz, the US 6 GHz band holds 59 {{us-6ghz-channels-20}}, against 25 in the 5 GHz band {{us-5ghz-channels-20}}. Every 6 GHz channel is new room for Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 devices, with no older devices slowing it down {{6ghz-no-legacy}}.

More channels let neighboring [[access-point|access points]], on the floors above and below and in the next unit, each use a channel of their own, so they compete less for [[airtime|airtime]]. That matters most where devices crowd together, such as emergency departments and busy nursing units.
beats.bottomLine: The 6 GHz band more than doubles the channels a hospital can spread its access points across.
beats.sceneDescription: Two roads leave the access point, divided into lanes of the same width, one lane per channel. The 5 GHz road has 25 lanes; the 6 GHz road beside it has 59 lanes and is more than twice as wide, with a car in every lane.

keyFigures.note: Other regions allow less; Europe harmonizes the lower part of the band.

sinceWifi6.wifi6: Uses the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands only; it cannot use 6 GHz{{6ghz-no-legacy}}.
sinceWifi6.wifi6e: Opens the 6 GHz band, free of older devices{{wifi6e-6ghz-origin}}.
sinceWifi6.wifi7: Adds 320 MHz channels, available only in 6 GHz{{eht-max-width}} {{320mhz-6ghz-only}}.
